paper.title: Machine-Learning-Guided Identification of Potent Osimertinib Analogues Targeting the EGFR Triple Mutant.
paper.abstract: Background: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations, including exon 19 deletions and L858R, are major drivers of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Although osimertinib is an established EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), the emergence of T790M and C797S mutations can reduce its effectiveness. This study aimed to identify and computationally prioritize osimertinib analogues with potential activity against the EGFR L858R/T790M/C797S triple mutant using an integrated machine-learning-assisted cheminformatics and structure-based approach. Methods: A library of 297,420 osimertinib analogues retrieved from PubChem was represented using physicochemical descriptors and 2048-bit Morgan fingerprints. Principal component analysis, t-SNE, UMAP, K-means clustering, and HDBSCAN were used to characterize chemical space, while Tanimoto similarity and Isolation Forest analysis were applied to assess structural similarity and scaffold novelty. Shortlisted compounds were subsequently evaluated using Glide extra-precision (XP) docking, induced-fit docking (IFD), molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Results: K-means analysis identified an osimertinib-containing cluster comprising 17,149 compounds, providing a focused chemical space for analogue prioritization. A clear inverse relationship was observed between Tanimoto similarity to osimertinib and quantitative estimate of drug-likeness (QED) among the top 30 compounds (Pearson's r = -0.86). Three compounds satisfied the predefined combination of Tanimoto similarity ≥ 0.4 and QED ≥ 0.5. Subsequent molecular modelling highlighted compounds 155515815 and 122474632, together with osimertinib, as compounds exhibiting favorable and stable interactions with key EGFR residues. MD simulations further supported the stability of the protein-ligand complexes, while DFT analysis provided additional insight into their electronic and molecular properties. Conclusions: The integrated machine-learning-assisted and structure-based workflow enabled systematic exploration of a large osimertinib analogue library and identified computationally prioritized candidates for further investigation against the EGFR L858R/T790M/C797S triple mutant. Compounds 155515815 and 122474632 showed favorable computational profiles across multiple analyses and may serve as starting points for further scaffold optimization. Experimental studies are required to determine their biological activity and potential to address osimertinib resistance.

paper.title: First-Line Treatment of EGFR-Mutated Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Osimertinib, Osimertinib Plus Chemotherapy, and Amivantamab Plus Lazertinib with Focus on Efficacy, Safety, Acquired Resistance, and Health-Economic Considerations.
paper.abstract: Background: Treatment of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) has evolved from first-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) to third-generation osimertinib and, more recently, to intensified first-line regimens. Osimertinib monotherapy remains effective and comparatively tolerable, while osimertinib plus platinum-pemetrexed and amivantamab plus lazertinib improve progression-free and overall survival at the cost of greater toxicity. This article evaluates current first- and subsequent-line treatment strategies for advanced NSCLC harboring common sensitizing EGFR mutations (exon 19 deletions or exon 21 L858R substitutions), with particular attention to efficacy, toxicity, resistance mechanisms, and patient selection. Methods: A structured assessment of phase III randomized trials, published network meta-analyses and indirect comparisons, and resistance-focused literature was conducted to compare efficacy, toxicity, resistance mechanisms, costs, and patient-selection considerations across current treatments. No original statistical analysis was performed; comparative estimates were derived from published studies. Results: First-line intensification with osimertinib plus chemotherapy or amivantamab plus lazertinib improves progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) over osimertinib alone in EGFR-mutant NSCLC, particularly in high-risk patients, but it also increases toxicity, and resistance remains heterogeneous and may require repeat molecular profiling to guide further therapy. Published indirect comparisons have not shown a significant difference between the two intensified regimens. Conclusions: No single regimen suits all patients. Fit patients with high-risk features may derive the greatest absolute benefit from first-line intensification. Apparent differences between osimertinib plus platinum-pemetrexed and amivantamab plus lazertinib in subgroups (such as L858R or TP53 co-mutation) are based mainly on exploratory cross-trial data and do not establish superiority of either regimen. Amivantamab plus lazertinib offers a chemotherapy-free alternative with a distinct toxicity profile. Osimertinib monotherapy remains appropriate for patients with lower-risk disease, frailty, poorer performance status, or significant comorbidities, or for those who prefer a lower treatment burden; age alone should not determine treatment choice. Post-progression therapy should be guided by repeat biopsy, plasma genotyping, and identified resistance mechanisms.

paper.title: Nuclear S100A4-HMGB1 promotes SLC7A11-dependent redox adaptation and ferroptosis tolerance in acquired osimertinib resistance.
paper.abstract: Acquired resistance limits the durable efficacy of osimertinib in epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but the redox adaptations that enable resistant cells to evade ferroptosis remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify nuclear S100A4 as a stress-responsive regulator of SLC7A11-dependent antioxidant defense during acquired osimertinib resistance. Osimertinib induces S100A4 through SP1-dependent transcriptional activation. S100A4 loss impairs cystine uptake and glutathione homeostasis, increases lipid peroxidation, and sensitizes cells to osimertinib, whereas its overexpression promotes resistance. Acute S100A4 depletion in independently generated resistant cells similarly increases lipid-peroxidative stress, reduces SLC7A11 expression, and restores osimertinib sensitivity. Ferroptosis inhibition substantially attenuates the sensitization caused by S100A4 loss, supporting ferroptosis as a functionally important component of S100A4-mediated resistance. Mechanistically, nuclear S100A4 interact with HMGB1 within an SLC7A11 promoter-associated chromatin complex, supporting SLC7A11 transcription. HMGB1 depletion impairs S100A4 occupancy at the SLC7A11 promoter, while S100A4 interaction-surface mutants reduce HMGB1 interaction and drug resistance. This regulatory program functionally converges with NRF2/ATF4 signaling, and SLC7A11 silencing attenuates S100A4-mediated osimertinib resistance. Paired pretreatment and post-progression specimens show coordinated increases in nuclear S100A4 and SLC7A11 following acquired EGFR-TKI resistance. Moreover, niclosamide increases ferroptotic stress and enhances osimertinib efficacy in resistant models, with genetic analyses indicating that S100A4 contributes to this sensitizing effect. Collectively, these findings identify a nuclear S100A4-HMGB1-SLC7A11 redox-adaptation program that contributes to ferroptosis tolerance and provides a rationale for exploiting redox vulnerabilities in osimertinib-resistant NSCLC.

paper.title: Discovery of HC9591, a selective macrocyclic EGFR C797S inhibitor with brain exposure in rats.
paper.abstract: Acquired epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) C797S mutations and brain metastases pose major challenges to the treatment of EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Here, we report HC9591, a brain-penetrant and wild-type (WT)-sparing macrocyclic EGFR C797S inhibitor discovered through physicochemical property-oriented linker optimization of our previously identified compound 7. HC9591 inhibited C797S-containing EGFR mutants with IC50 values of 0.27-3.53 nM, while showing substantially weaker inhibition of WT EGFR (IC50 = 632 nM) in biochemical assays. Cellular activity was further demonstrated in Ba/F3 cells expressing C797S-containing EGFR mutants (IC50 = 13.4-301 nM) and in the osimertinib-resistant PC-9-OR human lung cancer cell line (IC50 = 269 nM). HC9591 also demonstrated favorable pharmacokinetic properties in rats with an oral bioavailability of 39.6% and a half-life of 8.1 h. Importantly, HC9591 is brain-penetrant with a brain/plasma ratio of 0.46 in rats, and represents a promising lead against C797S-mediated osimertinib-resistant NSCLC.

paper.title: Integration of bulk and single-cell transcriptomics via the Scissor algorithm reveals APOE-dependent cholesterol metabolic reprogramming in macrophages associated with osimertinib resistance in non-small cell lung cancer.
paper.abstract: Background: The tumor microenvironment contributes to acquired resistance against osimertinib in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet the key cell subpopulations and the underlying metabolic mechanisms remain incompletely elucidated. Methods: The Scissor algorithm was applied to integrate bulk osimertinib-resistance transcriptomic profiles with single-cell RNA-seq data to pinpoint cell subpopulations functionally associated with the osimertinib resistant phenotype. AddModuleScore was applied to calculate scores for cholesterol metabolism-related modules. Gene-set enrichment analysis was carried out to uncover pathway alterations in osimertinib resistance-related macrophages. Cross-validation was performed in an independent dataset comparing treatment-naive and EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs)-treated progressive-disease lesions. EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma cells were treated with corresponding conditioned medium combined with osimertinib, followed by a panel of cell function assays, including cell proliferation, colony formation, and apoptosis. The gain- and loss- of function studies of APOE were conducted in THP-1 derived macrophages. Results: Osimertinib-resistant associated Scissor+ cells were mainly enriched within macrophages, which exhibited prominent APOE-dependent cholesterol metabolic reprogramming. APOE was markedly up-regulated in Scissor+ macrophages and macrophages from EGFR-TKI-treated progressive-disease lesions. Macrophage-derived APOE shapes extracellular cholesterol availability in the microenvironment, which may promote intracellular free-cholesterol accumulation in tumor cells and counteract osimertinib-triggered apoptosis. Conclusion: APOE-dependent cholesterol metabolic reprogramming in macrophages is associated with osimertinib resistance in NSCLC and may contribute to therapeutic failure. Our results identify APOE as a hypothesis-generating candidate molecule that merits further pre-clinical investigation.

paper.title: Efficacy and safety of third-generation EGFR-TKIs combined with local consolidative therapy as first-line treatment for EGFR-mutated stage IIIB-IV NSCLC: a retrospective study.
paper.abstract: Objective: Although third-generation EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs), such as osimertinib and aumolertinib, can improve prognosis as first-line treatment, most patients inevitably develop resistance and disease progression (PD). Local consolidative therapy (LCT) combined with TKIs can enhance therapeutic efficacy, but the existing evidence is mainly based on first- and second-generation TKIs. This retrospective case-control study aimed to evaluate whether the combination of LCT with third-generation EGFR-TKIs treatment can improve the efficacy and safety in the management of advanced NSCLC compared with TKIs monotherapy. Methods: This retrospective study enrolled patients diagnosed with EGFR-mutant NSCLC. The experimental group received EGFR-TKIs combined with LCT, and the control group received EGFR-TKIs monotherapy. The primary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS) and duration of objective response (DOR), which were compared using the Kaplan-Meier method and log-rank test; hazard ratios (HR) were analyzed by the Cox proportional hazards model. Subgroup analyses were conducted to investigate the heterogeneity. The patterns of PD and adverse events were summarized. Results: A total of 49 patients were enrolled in this study (combination therapy group: n = 27; monotherapy group: n = 22). The median PFS was significantly longer in the combination therapy group than in the monotherapy group (32.0 vs. 21.0 months; HR = 0.39, P = 0.012). The DOR was also superior in the combination therapy group (29.0 vs. 17.0 months; HR = 0.36, 95% CI: 0.16-0.78, P = 0.006). Subgroup analyses showed that significant PFS benefit from combination therapy can be observed in patients with extrathoracic metastasis and those who achieved partial response after TKI treatment. Multivariate Cox regression analysis identified combination local therapy (HR = 0.29, 95% CI: 0.12-0.70) and ≤ 5 metastatic lesions (HR = 0.12, 95% CI: 0.02-0.56) as independent prognostic factors for PFS. Analysis of disease progression patterns revealed that 87.5% of progression events in the combination therapy group occurred at sites not treated with LCT, while 80% of progression events in the monotherapy group arose from baseline pre-existing lesions. No statistically significant difference was found in the incidence of grade 1-2 and grade 3 adverse events between the two groups (all P > 0.05). Conclusion: Third-generation EGFR-TKIs combined with LCT can significantly prolong PFS and DOR in patients with advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC, with manageable safety.

paper.title: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor-producing lung squamous cell carcinoma positive for an uncommon EGFR Exon 20 S768I mutation: a case report.
paper.abstract: Background: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) lung carcinoma is a rare and highly aggressive clinical entity characterized by persistent neutrophilia, high fever, and poor prognosis. Although the lung is a common primary site, the co-occurrence of G-CSF production and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations is extremely rare, particularly in squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Case presentation: A 79-year-old Asian man, a former smoker, presented with an 80 mm mass in the left upper lobe and was diagnosed with a G-CSF-producing lung SCC (cT4N2bM0, cStage IIIB). Genetic testing identified a minor mutation and high programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression (tumor proportion score: TPS 65%). Despite an initial partial response to concurrent chemoradiotherapy, the disease progressed rapidly during maintenance durvalumab therapy, with a marked secondary increase in serum G-CSF and interleukin 6 (IL-6) levels. Subsequent lines of therapy, including docetaxel and the EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) afatinib and osimertinib, provided only transient or limited clinical benefits. The patient eventually succumbed to tumor progression 22 months after the initial diagnosis. Discussion: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first English-language report of a G-CSF-producing lung SCC harboring an EGFR S768I mutation. The present findings suggest that the inflammatory and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment associated with G-CSF and IL-6 production may contribute to resistance against both immune checkpoint inhibitors and EGFR-TKIs, even when targetable mutations are present. Conclusion: Although driver mutations are rare in G-CSF-producing lung carcinoma, their presence may not guarantee a good response to targeted therapies. This case underscores the need for careful treatment selection and highlights the importance of further research into the mechanisms of treatment resistance in this intractable phenotype.

paper.title: Disrupting ceramide glycosylation prevents adaptive resistance to osimertinib in in vitro and in vivo models of EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer.
paper.abstract: Acquired resistance to osimertinib remains a major limitation in the treatment of EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Increasing evidence indicates that sphingolipid metabolism remodelling contributes to drug tolerance and resistance in different cancers, including NSCLC. Here, we investigated whether the combination of an inhibitor of glucosylceramide synthase (GCS) with the EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitor osimertinib affects the development of resistance in EGFR-mutated NSCLC cells. The GCS inhibitor venglustat significantly reduces the emergence of osimertinib-resistant colonies after long-term exposure to osimertinib in EGFR-mutated NSCLC cell cultures. Combined treatment decreases drug-tolerant persister cell (DTP) survival and prevents regrowth after drug withdrawal. Genetic silencing of UDP-glucose:ceramide glucosyltransferase (UGCG) confirmed the role of GCS in osimertinib tolerance, reducing DTP survival and resistant colony formation. In a xenograft mouse model, the osimertinib-venglustat combination significantly reduces long-term tumour regrowth compared with osimertinib, without signs of toxicity. Untargeted MS lipidomics identified glycosylated ceramides (GlyCer) as major lipid species associated with resistance development. The concentration-dependent reduction in GlyCer upon GCS inhibition parallels decreased resistant colony formation. Further targeted MS analysis identified Gb3/Cer glycosylation ratio (GR) as a key feature associated with osimertinib resistance. A mechanistic relationship between glycosphingolipids and osimertinib resistance is supported by preliminary data showing increased Gb3 C16:0 GR in plasma from osimertinib-treated EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients at tumour progression compared with pre-treatment levels. These findings support the need for further investigation aimed at evaluating the combination of a GCS inhibitor with osimertinib to prevent the insurgence of resistance to first-line treatment of EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients.

paper.title: Epigenetically driven GAS2L3 enforces non-canonical cell cycle progression to promote osimertinib resistance in lung adenocarcinoma.
paper.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) have markedly improved outcomes in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), yet acquired resistance to the third-generation inhibitor osimertinib remains inevitable. Although metabolic reprogramming is increasingly recognized as a driver of therapeutic resistance, the epigenetic consequences of lactate accumulation and their functional relevance in osimertinib resistance are poorly understood. Here we report that osimertinib-resistant LUAD cells exhibit enhanced glycolytic flux, increased intracellular lactate levels, and elevated histone H4 lysine 8 lactylation (H4K8la). Integrative transcriptomic analysis revealed significant enrichment of cell-cycle-associated pathways in resistant tumors, despite downregulation of canonical Cyclin B1 and Cyclin D1. Among the upregulated genes, GAS2L3 emerged as a prominent candidate. Genome-wide CUT&Tag profiling demonstrated enrichment of H4K8la at the GAS2L3 promoter, which was confirmed by ChIP-qPCR. Functionally, GAS2L3 overexpression accelerated S/G2-M progression and promoted proliferation under drug pressure, whereas its silencing induced cell-cycle arrest and restored osimertinib sensitivity both in vitro and in xenograft models. Notably, resistant cells displayed elevated P53 expression without induction of its canonical effector P21, indicating checkpoint uncoupling and a noncanonical mode of cell-cycle regulation. Mechanistically, glycolysis inhibition reduced H4K8la and GAS2L3 expression and partially re-sensitized resistant cells, while exogenous lactate restored H4K8la levels and resistance phenotypes, establishing a metabolically driven epigenetic circuit. Clinically, high GAS2L3 expression was associated with shorter progression-free survival in osimertinib-treated patients. Collectively, our findings identify a glycolysis-H4K8la-GAS2L3 axis that drives noncanonical cell-cycle reprogramming independently of classical Cyclin-CDK activation, thereby promoting acquired osimertinib resistance. These results uncover a metabolism-epigenetics-cell cycle interface that may represent a therapeutic vulnerability in EGFR-mutant LUAD.

paper.title: Case Report: Longitudinal clonal evolution in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma with coexisting MET exon 14 skipping and EML4-ALK fusion and subsequent KRAS/BRAF bypass mutations.
paper.abstract: Acquired resistance to osimertinib in epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer occurs through on-target mutations or bypass activation of alternative pathways. The longitudinal molecular evolution of a tumor across successive lines of therapy is rarely captured by repeat biopsy. We report a 68-year-old never-smoking woman with EGFR exon 19 deletion lung adenocarcinoma. First-line therapy achieved a partial response, with progression after 10.7 months; after 61 months of osimertinib, re-biopsy revealed concurrent EGFR T790M (9.3%), EML4-ALK fusion (E6:A20; 6.0%), and MET exon 14 skipping (c.3028G>T; 4.0%); aumolertinib plus ensartinib achieved stable disease for approximately 13 months. On further progression, a third biopsy showed molecular changes consistent with clonal evolution: the EML4-ALK fusion, MET exon 14 alteration, and EGFR T790M were no longer detected; the EGFR exon 19 deletion expanded to 47.71%; and KRAS G12R (10.17%), KRAS L19F (7.85%), BRAF D594N (8.13%), and BRAF E501K (6.38%) had emerged. Treatment with ivonescimab, a programmed cell death protein 1 and vascular endothelial growth factor bispecific antibody, plus pemetrexed and carboplatin, followed by pemetrexed plus ivonescimab, achieved stable disease; because chemotherapy was given concurrently, the contribution of ivonescimab cannot be isolated. PD-L1 (tumor proportion score <1%) was assessed on an earlier biopsy and blood tumor mutational burden was measured in 2019. This case is consistent with longitudinal clonal dynamics under sequential targeted therapy, namely regression of drug-sensitive clones and emergence of mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway bypass alterations, and the feasibility of an immunotherapy-containing regimen in a multi-driver tumor with unfavorable immune biomarkers.

paper.title: Case Report: Long-term survival of a patient with lung adenocarcinoma harboring EGFR 19del/T790M/C797S and KIF26B-NTRK1 rearrangement.
paper.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene mutation stands as one of the most prevalent driver genetic alterations in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). While targeted therapies against EGFR have substantially enhanced patient prognosis, acquired resistance remains a core challenge that limits therapeutic efficacy. Patients with stage IV NSCLC generally exhibit a dismal prognosis, with only about 7% of those with stage IVB disease surviving beyond five years. Herein, we report a case of a 47-year-old female patient diagnosed with advanced lung adenocarcinoma, whose clinical course has persisted for nearly a decade. Initial genetic testing identified an EGFR exon 19 deletion (19del). Following treatment with osimertinib, the patient developed concurrent cis-arranged EGFR T790M/C797S double mutations and a neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase 1 (NTRK1) gene rearrangement. Subsequently, through a multimodal therapeutic strategy integrating local intervention, radiation therapy, and targeted therapy, the patient's disease has been sustainably controlled for several years, and she remains alive with stable clinical status to date. NTRK1 fusions are a well-defined mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR-TKIs, but they are uncommon. This case reports a KIF26B-NTRK1 rearrangement not previously described in lung cancer; however, its functional significance remains to be confirmed. The principal value of this report lies in the completeness of the longitudinal molecular and clinical record, which documents how an on-target mutation and a bypass rearrangement can coexist and persist.

paper.title: EGFR-Mutated Small Cell Lung Cancer: Molecular Characterization and Clinical Implications of EGFR-TKIs.
paper.abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is an aggressive neuroendocrine malignancy defined by a number of genetic and molecular features, including near-universal TP53 and RB1 inactivation, MYC amplifications, Notch pathway disruption, and hyperactivated PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling. The subtypes of SCLC, SCLC-A/N/P/I, are primarily based on four transcription regulators (ASCL1, NeuroD1, YAP1, POU). This review provides a concise overview of the molecular landscape of SCLC and then focuses on the subset displaying epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) alterations. EGFR-positive SCLC presents either as rare primary (de novo) disease (2.6-19.3%) or as transformed SCLC originating from EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in 3-14% of cases following EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy. In both cases, the tumors harbor EGFR mutations with the most frequent one being exon 19 deletions. A number of pathways have been identified regarding the lineage transformation with the co-occurring TP53 and RB1 loss predominating, while a number of other molecular mechanisms have been explored, including activation of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition factors (ZEB1, SLUG), MDM4 or BCL2L2/NFKBIA co-amplifications, and newly postulated genetic variants such as FBN1 and PALLD, alongside emergent surface expression of DLL3, B7-H3, and PTK7. Once SCLC transformation occurs, tumors tend to drop EGFR dependence and display profound resistance to EGFR-TKIs, necessitating a shift to standard platinum-etoposide chemotherapy, with or without immunotherapy. The value of EGFR-TKIs has been explored, as an add-on treatment, in several cases and its efficacy has not so far provided satisfactory outcomes. An update of the literature, within this particular field, is being provided along with the value for routine serial re-biopsy (tissue or liquid) upon disease progression, especially when EGFR-TKIs have been used. Early identification of neuroendocrine transformation can prevent futile EGFR-TKI monotherapy, capture mixed histologies, and recognize potential re-transformation back to adenocarcinoma.

paper.title: Advances in targeting the FGF-FGFR Pathway to overcome acquired EGFR-TKI resistance in non-small cell lung cancer.
paper.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality, and activating epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations define a clinically important molecular subtype. EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have substantially improved outcomes, but acquired resistance eventually limits long-term disease control. Among diverse resistance mechanisms, fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) signaling has emerged as one of several potential bypass pathways. This review summarizes evidence implicating fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) and FGFRs in selected contexts of resistance to EGFR inhibition. Genetic alterations, including receptor fusions, amplifications, and activating mutations, and non-genetic mechanisms such as receptor overexpression and ligand-driven autocrine signaling may sustain downstream pathway activation. These processes can reactivate mitogenic and survival signaling despite EGFR inhibition and may support tumor persistence in a subset of molecular settings. We discuss preclinical and clinical evidence for FGFR-associated resistance, with particular emphasis on the functionally characterized FGF2-FGFR1 axis. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including selective FGFR inhibitors, multi-kinase inhibitors, and investigational combination regimens with EGFR inhibitors or immunotherapy, are reviewed with attention to current limitations. Finally, we highlight challenges related to biomarker identification, routine testing, toxicity management, and clinical trial design, and outline future directions for evaluating FGFR-targeted approaches in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.

paper.title: The evolving immune ecosystem of TKI resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC: from treatment-induced remodeling to mechanism-guided therapy.
paper.abstract: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have transformed the treatment of EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet acquired resistance remains a major clinical limitation. Resistance is increasingly understood as an evolving state shaped not only by tumor-cell genomic alterations but also by treatment-induced remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). This Review examines how EGFR-TKI exposure reshapes macrophage states, T-cell function and localization, fibroblast and myeloid niches, and vascular architecture, and how these changes are reinforced by immune-checkpoint adaptation, metabolic reprogramming, and phenotypic plasticity. We then connect the evolving TIME to post-TKI therapeutic strategies according to the maturity of the supporting evidence, including immune checkpoint inhibitor-containing regimens, anti-angiogenic combinations, mechanism-matched targeted therapy, antibody-drug conjugates, bispecific T-cell engagers, and selected preclinical microenvironment-directed approaches. Finally, we discuss circulating biomarkers, single-cell sequencing, and spatial profiling as tools for longitudinally defining resistant immune states. Viewing TKI resistance as a temporally evolving immune ecosystem provides a framework for linking resistance mechanism, immune phenotype, and treatment selection rather than treating progression as a purely genomic endpoint.
